title: Planning a hen party dinner at your holiday house
summary: Plan a hen party dinner at your holiday house: budgets, menus, dietary needs and timings, with real yhangry booking data and a worked example.
body_markdown:
A dinner at your hen-party house gives the group a fixed point in the weekend: everyone comes back, sits down and spends time together. The organising is easier when one person handles the chef brief and the group agrees the budget early.


It is also the most common way to do it. Of the 1,672 UK hen and stag dinners booked through yhangry between 25 November 2025 and 24 November 2026, 85% were held in a rented property, and the typical group was 13 people (half of all groups had between 10 and 16).


Before you request menus, check the property permits an outside chef and that the dining space fits the people attending. The number of beds does not tell you how many guests can sit around the table.


## Agree the spending limit


Tell the group what the food budget covers and which costs are separate. Drinks, decorations, extra staff and equipment can change the total. If the dinner is part of a larger weekend budget, make that clear before anyone commits.


For a sense of scale: across those same 1,672 bookings, the median total paid was £724, and half of groups paid between £546 and £936. Per adult, the median was about £55, with half paying between £47 and £65 a head. These are past prices, not quotes. What you pay depends on the chef, menu, location and date, and our guide to[private chef costs for groups of 6, 10 and 20](https://yhangry.com/blog/private-chef-cost/) explains how group size changes the maths. It is also worth checking[what is included when you hire a private chef](https://yhangry.com/blog/whats-included-when-you-hire-a-private-chef/) before you split the cost, so nobody is surprised by a separate drinks or staff bill.


Collect the final headcount as early as possible. Ask the chef how changes affect the price and when numbers must be confirmed. Check the current payment options and our[terms for UK bookings](https://yhangry.com/blog/terms-and-conditions-2/) rather than promising the group a particular way to split the bill.


Leave yourself time, too. For the bookings above, the median gap between paying for the chef and the dinner itself was 70 days, and half were confirmed between 38 and 118 days ahead. That measures confirmed bookings, not first enquiries, so most organisers started looking even earlier.


## Pick food the group will enjoy


Start with the bride’s preferences, then consider how the whole table likes to eat. Sharing dishes can suit a lively evening; a plated menu gives the meal a more structured pace. If the group likes the idea of a feast in the middle of the table, Chef Mark’s[Filipino kamayan dinners](https://yhangry.com/kamayan-at-home-chef-mark-rise-via-private-dining/) show how far a sharing format can go. Ask the chef what works in the house and within your budget.


Collect dietary requirements privately and accurately, and share the relevant details with the chef. If someone has an allergy, arrange clarification before confirming their meal. A vegan or plant-based guest should get a dish that feels like part of the meal, not an afterthought;[Chef Nicole’s plant-based menus](https://yhangry.com/nicole-plant-based-menus-yhangry/) are a good example of what to ask for. Avoid asking the group to negotiate complicated menu changes in a busy chat on the day.


## Check the house before booking


Share photographs of the kitchen, appliances, table and available crockery. Ask who supplies anything missing and whether it needs to be hired. Our[checklist of what kitchen a private chef needs](https://yhangry.com/blog/private-chef-kitchen-requirements/) covers the details chefs usually ask about. Confirm parking and access so the chef can unload without the organiser leaving another activity halfway through.


If you have only just checked in, allow time to inspect the kitchen and clear space. Someone needs to be present at the chef’s agreed arrival time with the necessary access information. Our[holiday cottage planning checklist](https://yhangry.com/blog/private-chef-holiday-cottage-checklist/) walks through the arrival day step by step.


## Make the timetable realistic


Tell the chef when the group will return from activities and when you hope to eat. Leave a sensible margin for travel and getting ready. If you want games or speeches during dinner, agree where they fit around service.


Choose one person to handle questions on the night. That lets the bride and the rest of the group enjoy the evening without several people giving conflicting instructions.


## Learn from a real hen dinner


In November 2026, a group of 14 booked[Chef Jake B](https://yhangry.com/booking/chef/jake-b-6/) to cook a hen do dinner at a rented holiday house in Cockermouth, Cumbria. The brief was short and specific: a three-course meal, a red-carpet theme inspired by *Bridgerton* , Italian or fine-dining food for the starter and main, and a note that the bride loves tiramisu.


Jake’s menu gave the group a choice at every course:

The total was £782, or about £56 a head, close to the £55 median for UK hen and stag dinners over the past year. There were no separate waiting staff: according to the host’s review, Jake served every course himself, arrived on time, and left the kitchen tidy. The host said every option on the menu went down well and that the cooking made their weekend.


What made it work was the brief. It named the bride’s favourite dessert, a cuisine and a theme, which gave the chef enough to build a menu around without a long back-and-forth. This is one real booking shared as an example, not a quote.


The best brief is usually straightforward: who is coming, where you are staying, what you want to spend and the kind of food the bride loves.[Send those details through yhangry](https://yhangry.com/booking/quote/) and compare the full chef proposals before choosing.


### You might also like


Frequently asked questions


How much does a private chef cost for a hen party dinner?


Around £55 a head is typical. Half of the hen and stag dinners booked through yhangry last year came in between £47 and £65 per person. Your chef, menu and location set the final price, and drinks are extra.


How far ahead should we book?


Two to three months before the weekend, if you can. The typical group confirms its chef about ten weeks ahead.


Can a private chef cook in a holiday house or Airbnb?


Yes, and most hen dinners are booked that way. Check the house allows an outside chef, then send the chef photos of the kitchen and dining table. Here’s[what a chef needs from the kitchen](https://yhangry.com/blog/private-chef-kitchen-requirements/) .


Can the chef cater for different dietary needs?


Yes. Include everyone’s requirements in your brief and flag allergies clearly, so the chef can confirm how they’ll handle them before you book. Ask for vegan or vegetarian options to be part of the main menu, so nobody feels left out.
